descricao: Body parts organized as natural pairs — head and face, upper body, arms and legs — plus action verbs, the grammar of body-part sentences, and words that behave unexpectedly.

secoes.conteudo:
Here is a situation that happens to everyone. You are with a doctor, a physiotherapist, or a pharmacist — and they ask: 'Where exactly does it hurt?' You know exactly which part of your body is the problem. But you cannot find the word in English. So you point and hope. That works sometimes — but not always.

Knowing the names of body parts is one of the most practical things you can learn in any language. And in English, most of them follow a logic that makes them easier to learn as pairs. The body is full of matching structures: two sides, joints that mirror each other, parts that connect in sequence. In this material, you will learn the vocabulary by following those natural pairs — head / face, upper / lower body, arm / leg — so that each word brings another word with it.

secoes.titulo: Head and Face: Forehead / Chin, Eye / Ear, Cheek / Temple
secoes.conteudo:
Let's start at the top. The **head** is the entire upper structure. On the front of your head: your **face**. The **forehead** is the smooth area above your eyes — the wide, flat surface that shows expression most clearly. At the opposite end of the face, below your mouth: your **chin**. These two — **forehead** and **chin** — mark the full vertical span of the face, one at the top, one at the bottom.

In between: your **cheeks** — the soft, rounded areas on either side of your nose and mouth. And on the sides, where your face meets your hairline: your **temples** — the flat, slightly sunken areas right beside your eyes. Cheek and temple are both on the side of the face, but at different depths: the **cheek** is forward-facing, the **temple** is to the side.

Your **eyes** and **ears** are a natural pair — one for seeing, one for hearing. Each **eye** is framed by **eyelashes** along the edge and **eyebrows** — the arched lines of hair just above. Your **ears** sit on both sides of the head. Between your eyes: your **nose**. Below your nose: your **mouth**, with two **lips** — top and bottom — and **teeth** inside. One **tooth**, many **teeth** — one of the two most important irregular plurals in body vocabulary. Say it out loud until it is automatic: tooth, teeth.

Your **neck** connects your head to your body. The front and inner part of your neck — the passage for food and air — is your **throat**. When it is sore and painful, usually from a cold or infection, you have a **sore throat**. That phrase is one of the most commonly used descriptions of illness in everyday English.

secoes.titulo: Upper Body: Chest / Back, Shoulder / Hip, Waist / Neck
secoes.conteudo:
Below the neck, the torso has a front and a back, and anchor points where the limbs attach.

The front of your upper body is your **chest**. The rear surface — what faces behind you — is your **back**. These two are among the most used body words in everyday English: 'my chest hurts,' 'I have a bad back,' 'she carried it on her back.' Simple, clear, and essential.

At the top of the torso: your **shoulders** — the rounded joints where your arms connect to your body. At the bottom: your **hips** — the wide, bony structures on each side of your lower body, where your legs begin. **Shoulder** and **hip** mirror each other perfectly: both are attachment points for limbs, one at the top, one at the bottom.

Between chest and hips: your **stomach** — the soft area in the front. In casual speech, this area is also called your **belly**, and the two words are interchangeable in everyday conversation. Your **waist** is the narrower section in the middle of the torso — the area where a belt sits. 'She has a small waist,' 'he tightened the belt around his waist' — this word comes up often in descriptions and clothing.

secoes.titulo: Arms and Legs: Elbow / Knee, Wrist / Ankle, Finger / Toe
secoes.conteudo:
The arms and legs are the body's most perfectly matched structures: each limb has the same sequence of joints from shoulder or hip to fingertip or toe.

Your **arms** and **legs** are the four main limbs. Each **arm** runs from the shoulder to the **hand**. Each **leg** runs from the hip down to the **foot** — and here is the second essential irregular plural: one **foot**, two **feet**. Never 'foots.' Say it until it is automatic: foot, feet.

In the middle of each arm: the **elbow** — the joint where the arm bends. In the middle of each leg: the **knee** — the joint where the leg bends. **Elbow** and **knee** form a perfect pair: both are bending joints, both sit in the middle of their limb. If you learn one, you understand why the other exists.

At the end of each arm, just before the hand: the **wrist** — the joint connecting arm to hand. At the end of each leg, just before the foot: the **ankle** — the joint connecting leg to foot. **Wrist** and **ankle** mirror each other exactly. The simplest rule: **wrist** is on the arm, **ankle** is on the leg.

Your **hand** has four **fingers** and one **thumb** — the short, thick digit on the side. The **thumb** is not called a finger in English; it has its own name. Your **foot** has five **toes** — the equivalent of fingers for the foot. **Finger** and **toe** are the natural pair: digits, one set at each extremity. The **palm** is the flat inner surface of your hand. The **sole** is the flat underside of your foot. **Palm** and **sole** mirror each other exactly — one on the hand, one on the foot.

secoes.titulo: What the Body Does: Verbs of Action and Gesture
secoes.conteudo:
The body is not just a collection of parts — it does things. And many of those actions have specific verbs that are essential at B1 level.

With the hands: you **clap** when you bring both palms together repeatedly — to show appreciation or keep rhythm. You **wave** to greet or say goodbye from a distance, moving your hand from side to side. You **point** to show where something is, using your index finger — the finger right next to the **thumb**. You **grab** something when you take hold of it quickly and firmly. You **snap** your fingers to emphasize a moment or get someone's attention.

With the face: your **eyes** **blink** automatically — they close and open very quickly every few seconds without you thinking about it. You **smile** when you are happy, using your **mouth** and **face** together. You **nod** — move your **head** down and then up — to show agreement or say yes. You **shake** your head — move it from side to side — to say no. These two gestures, nodding and shaking the head, are worth knowing by name.

With the full body: you **stretch** to extend a muscle as far as it will comfortably go — the feeling of waking up in the morning. You **bend** when you curve a part of your body — you bend your **knees**, bend your **arm**, bend forward to pick something up. **Straighten** is the opposite: you make a bent part straight again. You **raise** something to lift it upward — raise your **hand**, raise your **arm**, raise your **eyebrows**.

For seeing: you **see** something without trying — your **eyes** simply register it. You **look** at something on purpose — you direct your **eyes** intentionally. You **watch** something that moves or unfolds over time — a film, a match, a person. Three verbs, all connected to your **eyes**, all with different meanings.

Here is a small but important difference between English and Portuguese that most learners do not notice until someone points it out.

In English, when you talk about pain or injury to a body part, you use a possessive pronoun — my, his, her, our — not the definite article 'the.'

'My back hurts.' Not 'The back hurts.'
'She hurt her knee.' Not 'She hurt the knee.'
'He broke his arm.' Not 'He broke the arm.'

In Portuguese, the definite article is natural in these sentences: 'Ela machucou o joelho.' In English, the possessive is required. The body belongs to someone, and English insists you say whose.

This matters because the mistake is nearly invisible — if you say 'I hurt the shoulder,' English speakers understand you. But the moment you switch to 'I hurt my shoulder,' you sound completely fluent. It is one of those small changes that makes a large difference.

The same pattern applies to symptoms and complaints. In English, you say 'I have a headache' — not 'my head hurts,' though that is also valid. 'She has a sore throat.' 'He has a stomachache.' These fixed phrases — 'have a' plus a body-related complaint — are the standard way to describe pain and illness in everyday English. Learn them as complete phrases, not as constructions you need to build each time.

A few body vocabulary words behave unexpectedly — either because they sound like something else, or because one English word covers what Portuguese splits into two.

**Calf** is the muscle at the back of your lower leg — the large, rounded muscle you feel when you stand on your toes. It is also the English word for a young cow. Context resolves this instantly: 'I pulled my calf in training' is clearly about a leg muscle. But knowing the double meaning prevents surprise when you see it in a different context.

**Chest** is the front of your upper body. It is also a large box for storage — a treasure chest, a wooden chest full of old things. Again, context tells you immediately which one: 'my chest hurts' versus 'the chest is full of photographs.' Two completely different things, one word.

**Ear** covers the full hearing organ in English. In Portuguese, there is a distinction: 'orelha' for the external, visible ear and 'ouvido' for the inner ear or the sense of hearing. English collapses both into **ear**. 'My ear hurts' covers everything from the outer structure to deep internal pain. If you need to specify, you say 'outer ear' or 'inner ear' — but in everyday speech, just **ear** is enough.

**Tooth** and **teeth**. **Foot** and **feet**. Say these out loud until they feel automatic: one tooth, many teeth. One foot, two feet. Not 'tooths,' not 'foots.' These are the two irregular plurals that come up most in body vocabulary, and getting them right is one of the clearest signs of a careful learner.
